# Version Control with Git and GitHub for Automation Projects

##### The folder called "final_v3_ACTUAL_use_this"

Every self-taught developer has this folder. Inside it: `scraper.py`, `scraper_new.py`, `scraper_fixed.py`, `scraper_fixed_WORKING.py`, and a file called `scraper_backup_before_i_broke_it.py` dated three weeks ago.

Then something breaks in production. You know it worked on Tuesday. You do not know which file was running on Tuesday, what you changed since, or why. You start opening files and comparing them by eye.

**Git** ends this permanently. It records every version of every file with a message explaining why it changed, lets you return to any point in history, and lets you experiment without risking what works. **GitHub** puts that history in the cloud, makes it shareable, and — for someone building a career — turns your work into a portfolio a hiring manager can actually browse.

For an automation engineer specifically, Git matters for three reasons: your Python scripts are code, your exported workflow JSON is code, and your credentials must never accidentally become public — and Git, used properly, is what prevents that.

##### The core model

Git tracks **snapshots**. Each snapshot — a **commit** — records the state of your files plus a message, an author and a timestamp. Commits form a chain, and you can move along that chain.

Files live in one of four states:

```text
working directory  →  staging area  →  local repository  →  remote (GitHub)
   (you edit)         (git add)          (git commit)         (git push)
```

The staging area exists so you can commit *some* changes and not others — useful when you have fixed a bug and started an unrelated experiment in the same session.

##### The commands you need

Setting up, once per machine:

```bash
git config --global user.name  "Ananya Rao"
git config --global user.email "ananya@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

Starting a project:

```bash
mkdir automation-portfolio && cd automation-portfolio
git init                             # create the repository

# create .gitignore FIRST — before any secret exists
cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
.env
.env.local
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
credentials.json
*.log
data/raw/
EOF

git add .gitignore
git commit -m "chore: add gitignore for secrets and build artefacts"
```

The daily loop:

```bash
git status                           # what changed? — run this constantly
git diff                             # exactly what changed, line by line
git add weather_report.py            # stage one file
git add .                            # stage everything (check status first!)
git commit -m "feat: fetch weather for three cities and write CSV"
git log --oneline --graph            # readable history
```

Undoing things — the reason Git is worth learning:

```bash
git restore weather_report.py        # discard uncommitted changes to a file
git restore --staged weather.py      # unstage but keep the changes
git commit --amend -m "better msg"   # fix the most recent commit message
git revert a1b2c3d                   # new commit that undoes an old one (safe)
git checkout a1b2c3d -- script.py    # recover one file from an old commit
```

**Commit messages matter.** "update" tells your future self nothing. The convention many teams use is a type prefix plus a plain description:

```text
feat: add retry with exponential backoff to the API sync
fix: handle empty items array in order webhook
docs: document environment variables in README
chore: bump requests to 2.32.0
refactor: extract clean_record into its own function
```

Aim for commits that are **one logical change**. A commit touching eleven unrelated things cannot be reverted cleanly.

##### Branches and merging

A **branch** is an independent line of development. You create one, make changes freely, and `main` stays untouched and working the whole time.

```bash
git switch -c feature/add-slack-alerts    # create and switch to a branch
# ... edit, add, commit as usual ...
git switch main                           # back to main
git merge feature/add-slack-alerts        # bring the work in
git branch -d feature/add-slack-alerts    # tidy up
```

```mermaid
gitGraph
    commit id: "init"
    commit id: "add scraper"
    branch feature/slack-alerts
    commit id: "add slack client"
    commit id: "wire alerts to errors"
    checkout main
    commit id: "fix csv encoding"
    merge feature/slack-alerts
    commit id: "release v1"
```

The value for an automation engineer is concrete: you can rewrite a working sync script on a branch, test it thoroughly, and merge only when it passes — while the version running in production remains exactly as it was.

**Merge conflicts** happen when two branches change the same lines. Git marks them in the file:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
retry_attempts = 3
=======
retry_attempts = 5
>>>>>>> feature/add-slack-alerts
```

You edit the file to the version you want, delete the marker lines, then `git add` and `git commit`. Conflicts feel alarming the first time and become routine by the fifth.

##### GitHub and pull requests

GitHub hosts your repository remotely. Connect a local repo to it:

```bash
gh repo create automation-portfolio --public --source=. --push
# or manually:
git remote add origin https://github.com/<you>/automation-portfolio.git
git push -u origin main
```

Then daily:

```bash
git push          # send your commits up
git pull          # bring others' commits down
git clone <url>   # get a copy of an existing repo
```

A **pull request (PR)** is a proposal: "here are the commits on my branch — please review and merge them into `main`." It is the unit of collaboration in professional software teams, and it gives you a place for discussion, review comments, and automated checks before code reaches the main branch.

```bash
git switch -c fix/timezone-bug
# ... commit your work ...
git push -u origin fix/timezone-bug
gh pr create --title "fix: use Asia/Kolkata for report window" \
             --body "Report was computing yesterday in UTC, shifting the window by 5.5 hours."
```

Even working solo, PRs are worth using. They force you to read your own diff before merging, which catches an astonishing number of mistakes — including committed secrets.

##### Versioning exported workflows

Here is the part specific to your discipline, and it is a genuine differentiator.

Your n8n, Make and Zapier workflows are **also code** — they just live inside a web UI. Export them and commit them:

- **n8n** — workflow menu → *Download*, producing a JSON file. Credentials are referenced by name, not embedded.
- **Make.com** — scenario menu → *Export Blueprint*, also JSON.
- **Zapier** — no clean export, so document the structure in Markdown with screenshots.

A well-structured repository looks like this:

```text
automation-portfolio/
├── README.md                    # what each automation does, how to run it
├── .gitignore                   # .env, .venv, __pycache__, data/raw
├── .env.example                 # variable NAMES only, no values
├── requirements.txt
├── scripts/
│   ├── weather_report.py
│   └── lead_cleaner.py
├── workflows/
│   ├── n8n/lead-capture.json
│   └── make/order-sync.blueprint.json
└── docs/
    ├── lead-capture.md          # trigger, steps, failure modes
    └── architecture.md
```

Committing workflow JSON gives you version history for visual automations — you can diff two versions to see exactly which node changed, and restore a working version after a bad edit. Very few junior candidates do this, and it reads as real engineering maturity.

**Before committing an exported workflow, open the JSON and search it** for `api`, `key`, `token`, `secret` and `password`. Exports are usually clean, but a key typed directly into an HTTP node's header field (rather than stored as a credential) *will* be in there.

##### .gitignore and why leaked keys are so dangerous

`.gitignore` lists patterns Git should never track. Anything matching stays on your machine and out of the repository.

The reason this is critical: **Git history is permanent by default.** If you commit a secret and delete it in the next commit, it is still in the history, still visible in `git log -p`, still in every clone anyone made. Removing it properly requires rewriting history (`git filter-repo` or BFG), force-pushing, and coordinating with everyone who has a copy.

Meanwhile, automated scanners crawl public GitHub continuously looking for credential patterns. Real-world measurements consistently find keys being exploited within *minutes* of being pushed. There are well-documented cases of five-figure cloud bills accrued overnight from a single leaked key.

So the rules are:

1. Write `.gitignore` **before** you create `.env`.
2. Run `git status` before every commit and actually read the file list.
3. Commit `.env.example` with names and empty values so collaborators know what to set.
4. Enable GitHub's secret scanning and push protection (free on public repos).
5. If you do leak a key: **revoke and rotate it immediately** — that is the real fix. Cleaning history is secondary, because the key is already compromised.

##### Common pitfalls

- **`git add .` without checking `git status`** — the classic way secrets get committed.
- **Committing `.venv/` or `node_modules/`** — thousands of files, huge repo.
- **Messages like "update" or "fix"** — useless six months later.
- **Giant commits** mixing unrelated changes.
- **Working directly on `main`** for risky changes.
- **Never pushing** — a local-only repo is not a backup.
- **`git push --force` on a shared branch** — overwrites other people's work.
- **Committing large data files** — use `data/` in `.gitignore` and keep samples small.

##### Your hands-on tie-in

The practical task walks the whole cycle: create a GitHub repository for your automation work, `git init` locally, commit your **Day 21 script**, add a **`.gitignore` excluding `.env`**, create a **branch**, make a change, and **merge it back**. Do the `.gitignore` first. Then run `git log --oneline --graph` and look at what you built — a real, inspectable history.

The mini project is your portfolio foundation: a **well-structured repository** containing your scripts and at least one **exported workflow JSON**, with a clear **README**, a `.gitignore` for secrets, and a history of **meaningful commits**. Write the README for a stranger: what each automation does, what problem it solves, which environment variables it needs, and how to run it. This repository is something you can put on a résumé, and the workflow exports will make it stand out.

For the assignment, explain **commit, branch and pull request in your own words**, and describe **why committing an API key is dangerous and how `.gitignore` prevents it**. Emphasize permanence — deleting the line does not remove it from history — and automated scanning. Finish with the correct response to a leak: revoke and rotate first, clean history second.

##### Key takeaways

- Git records every version with a reason; commits are snapshots, and you can always return to a working state.
- The loop is `status` → `add` → `commit` → `push`, with clear, single-purpose commit messages.
- Branches let you build and test risky changes without touching working code; pull requests add review, discussion and a final look at your own diff.
- Export and commit your n8n/Make workflow JSON — visual automations deserve version history too, and doing so signals real maturity.
- Write `.gitignore` before your first secret exists, never commit `.env`, and if a key leaks, revoke and rotate it immediately.
